item.title: Las Meninas
item.lesson: The five-year-old Infanta Margarita stands in a shaft of light, attended by her maids of honor — las meninas — a dwarf, a mastiff, and, at his easel at the left, Velázquez himself, brush poised, looking directly at you. On the back wall a mirror reflects the king and queen of Spain, standing exactly where you stand. So who is being painted? The princess? The royal couple? You? Velázquez folds painter, subject, and viewer into a single knot that philosophers — most famously Michel Foucault, who opened a book with it — have been untying ever since. It is also, plainly, the most virtuosic brushwork of the Spanish Golden Age: up close the Infanta's hair is a few dragged strokes; step back and it is silk and light. Luca Giordano called it 'the theology of painting.' The red cross of the Order of Santiago on Velázquez's chest was added after the fact — legend says the king himself painted it — a knighthood the painter chased for decades because painting was not yet considered a noble art. This picture settled the argument.
item.lookFor: Find the man in the lit doorway at the back, pausing on the stair. He is the picture's escape hatch — the one point where the closed room opens to somewhere else, and he cannot decide if he is coming or going.
